title: Vectors, What Even Are They? (3Blue1Brown Essence of Linear Algebra Ch. 1)
hook: A provocative opening quote — 'The introduction of numbers as coordinates is an act of violence' — frames the entire video as a reconciliation between two ways of seeing, earning curiosity before a single vector is drawn.

scenes.purpose: Establish the central tension: three valid but conflicting conceptions of a vector

on_screen.desc: Opening quote from Hermann Weyl in green highlight
Three Pi Creature characters (physicist pink, CS purple, mathematician) with labels
Number plane with a yellow vector and coordinate label introduced then faded

scenes.transition: Plane and labels fade out; three characters remain as anchors for each perspective
scenes.narration_gist: There are three distinct but related ideas about what a vector is — physics, CS, and mathematics — and reconciling them is the point.

scenes.purpose: Concretize the physics perspective: vectors as arrows with length and direction

on_screen.desc: Physicist Pi Creature in speaking mode
Single arrow rotating and moving to show length/direction independence
'Two-dimensional' label in corner

scenes.transition: Other two characters fade out; random colored vectors appear then disappear; label swaps to 'Three-dimensional'
scenes.narration_gist: A vector is an arrow in space — what defines it is length and direction, not position.

scenes.purpose: Concretize the CS perspective: vectors as ordered lists, order matters

on_screen.desc: CS student Pi Creature in sassy mode
House SVG icon with square footage (red) and price (green) labels
Column vector with footage/price entries; ≠ swapped version showing order matters

scenes.transition: House and vector slide off-screen left; all three characters restored to plain mode
scenes.narration_gist: A vector is an ordered list of numbers — model a house as [sq ft, price] and the order is part of the meaning.

scenes.purpose: Introduce the mathematician's view briefly, then explicitly defer it

on_screen.desc: Mathematician Pi Creature pondering
v and w arrows with tip-to-tail sum arrow in green
Array addition equation and scalar multiplication side by side
'We'll ignore him for now' with circle drawn around abstract symbols

scenes.transition: Circle drawn dismissing abstraction; scene clears to single-thought framing scene
scenes.narration_gist: The mathematician sees vectors as anything supporting addition and scalar multiplication — we'll set that aside and work concretely.

scenes.purpose: Fix the one mental image the viewer should hold throughout the series

on_screen.desc: Single yellow vector rooted at origin on number plane
xy coordinate plane with axis labels
Tail label with pointer line to origin dot

scenes.transition: Tail label fades; vector dramatically arcs away from origin and snaps back, reinforcing 'rooted at origin' rule
scenes.narration_gist: Always picture a vector as an arrow with its tail fixed at the origin of a coordinate system.

scenes.purpose: Walk through the coordinate system and show how coordinates instruct movement

on_screen.desc: x-axis then y-axis built up with tick marks and unit brace labeled '1'
Vector [-2,3] with colored x-line (red) and y-line (yellow) showing step path
Column vector bracket label with colored coordinate entries

scenes.transition: Scene clears back to axes only; 3D extension mentioned verbally with z-axis label written large
scenes.narration_gist: The two numbers in a vector's coordinates are instructions: walk this far along x, then this far parallel to y.

scenes.purpose: Define vector addition geometrically then verify it numerically

on_screen.desc: v (yellow) and w (maroon) arrows; w shifts to tip of v for tip-to-tail addition
Sum vector (pink) drawn from origin to tip of repositioned w
Column vector sum [1,2]+[3,-1]=[1+3, 2+(-1)] built step by step

scenes.transition: Why-question posed with alternative wrong sum shown; answered by walking a Randolph figure along each vector
scenes.narration_gist: To add vectors, place the second's tail at the first's tip; the sum is the shortcut arrow — and numerically, just add corresponding components.

scenes.purpose: Define scalar multiplication through visual stretching, squishing, and flipping

on_screen.desc: Vector v stretched to 2v, squished to (1/3)v, flipped and scaled to -1.8v
Scalar factor (2, 1/3, -1.8) written upper left before each transform
'Scaling' and 'Scalars' labels with example list

scenes.transition: Each example clears back to original vector before next; final scene shows numeric verification with 2·[3,1]=[6,2]
scenes.narration_gist: Multiplying a vector by a scalar stretches or flips it, and numerically means multiplying every component by that scalar.

scenes.purpose: Synthesize both perspectives as equally valid, valuable for translation between them

on_screen.desc: Physicist and CS student Pi Creatures exchanging speech bubbles
Arrow with x/y component lines shown alongside column vector, double arrow between them
Data grid of numbers transforming into vectors on a plane forming an ellipse

scenes.transition: Space-manipulation animation (wave homotopy + linear transform) demonstrates power of numeric-geometric translation
scenes.narration_gist: Neither perspective is more fundamental — the power of linear algebra comes from freely translating between the geometric and numerical views.

scenes.purpose: Tease next video and close the loop

on_screen.desc: 'Next video: Linear combinations, span, and bases'
Blue rectangle placeholder for next video thumbnail

scenes.transition: Everything fades; rectangle grows to fill stage
scenes.narration_gist: Now that we have vector basics, next we'll explore span, bases, and linear dependence.

lessons: Open with a conceptual conflict or provocative quote to make the viewer feel a tension worth resolving before any content is shown.
Assign each competing idea its own persistent visual anchor (a character, a color, a zone) so the viewer always knows whose perspective is on screen.
Defer abstract generalizations explicitly and on-screen — naming what you are skipping and why earns trust and keeps pacing tight.
Fix one canonical mental image early (vector rooted at origin) and physically demonstrate breaking then restoring that rule to make it stick.
Alternate between geometric and numeric representations of the same operation in the same scene so viewers build the translation reflex, not just one view.
Use a walking figure or animated step path through a diagram to turn abstract coordinate instructions into felt, embodied movement.
Reserve the conclusion_band for synthesis statements that explicitly name the transferable principle, not just a restatement of the example.
